title: What if we just gave up on homework?
author: Eric Hudson
summary: Eric Hudson starts from a senior who admits she has not read a full book for school since freshman year and from a growing trend of teachers who have stopped grading, collecting or even assigning homework because of AI. He uses Dan Meyer's proposed grading policy, in which exams count for 80 percent, homework is complete or incomplete, and AI use is allowed, as a case study of refusing to police what cannot be verified. Hudson argues that AI is a chance to return homework to its purpose as practice and recommends three principles: do not grade it, treat it as an occasion for feedback, and design it for student agency. He draws on Joe Feldman, Daniel Willingham, Pooja Agarwal, Colleen Ferguson and Denise Pope, and notes that cheating has not surged but AI is simply a new shortcut. For writing-heavy subjects he sketches an English classroom with social annotation, in-class reading and free writing, and explain-it-to-me checks. His closing stance is that no strategy is AI-proof, and the goal is to make the work worth doing. The piece is classified Ed-Tech because AI is the trigger and the policy question, though it also fits Learning & Curriculum.
points: Because AI makes unsupervised practice optional, the sensible response is to assess what can be verified in class and stop policing what happens outside it.
Grading homework mostly enforces compliance; low-weight or ungraded practice keeps final grades accurate and protects teacher-student relationships.
Frequent, low-stakes retrieval mini-quizzes tell students how much a piece of homework helped them, which shifts AI conversations from discipline to self-regulation.
Homework design drives offloading: rote, poorly explained or mismatched tasks invite shortcuts, so Colleen Ferguson's motivation, capacity and opportunity test is a useful audit.
In writing classes, more social annotation, in-class reading and free writing plus a requirement to explain your work replace AI bans.
quotes: If I had to identify a new trend I’m seeing in my work since this school year began, it’s teachers’ more openly questioning the purpose of homework. Because of AI, some teachers have stopped grading homework.

Meyer makes a clear and pragmatic refusal to try to police student behavior on AI. He acknowledges the reality (backed up by data) that policing student use of AI outside of class is exhausting and can be costly to teacher-student relationships. Instead, he will assess what he can verify.
There is an opportunity in all of this frustration and disruption: letting go of homework as a tool for compliance and holding on to its potential as a tool for learning.

Feldman argues that grading a student on whether they do their homework is more about enforcing compliance than assessing learning. He further argues that counting homework performance towards the final grade misses the point of a grade, which is to demonstrate what a student has learned as a result of weeks or months of learning.

In the true spirit of assessment, these quizzes should not be designed to “catch” students seeking shortcuts; they should offer the student information about how much they benefited from the homework, regardless of how they did the homework.
Conversations about AI stop being about disciplinary action and start being about self-regulation. Feedback is focused on teaching the student how to learn, not simply to verify if they did the work.

Pope suggests educators stop focusing on the quantity of homework and their policing of it (the same shift Meyer is making), and start using their time to ensure they are designing it in a way that incentivizes student engagement.
I would be transparent that the work I ask them to do is designed to make their thinking visible, not police their use of AI. And I would not ban the use of AI in out-of-class assignments.
